messages.subject: Variance structure
parts:
I have been having some trouble implementing a variance structure for a fairly simple linear model of some vegetation cover data using rstan. It is possible I am getting something very basic wrong here and I would appreciate any advise or guidance. 

I have two response variables I would like to model separately (y1 and y2 in the attached data), they are different ways of calculating relative dominance of species in plots. I have drastically simplified the model and data to try and trouble shoot here, but the basic problem remains the same. The data consists of 1573 observations of 15 species in 261 plots, with not all species occurring in all plots. I started by simply modeling the response variable as a linear combination of an intercept, a predictor variable, x, and random effects of species and plot. The problem arises when I attempt to include a variance structure, where the modeled mean response variable has a unique variance for each species (similar to the varIdent parameter in the nlme package in R). Including this variance structure appears to work fine for one of the modeled response variables, but not the other. In the one that does not work I end up with huge Rhat values and low neff (2). When I look at the parameter traces for the model that does not work the chains for most parameters seem to start off mixing, but then drift to separate values and almost completely stop varying during sampling. Interestingly, if I remove the random effect of "plot", but leave in the variance structure (which is based on species) the model seems to behave. I can not seem to figure out why the behavior is so different for the two response variables. The only obvious difference between the two response variables is that the problematic one is much less variable within plots (in some plots all species have the same value, leading to zero variation between species in that plot), but this does not seem to cause a problem when I do not include the variance structure based on species. 

The meat of the stan model looks like this:

parameters{
  real alpha;
  real beta;
  vector[15] sppran; //random effect of species
  vector[261] plotran; //random effect of plot
  real<lower = 0, upper = 100> sigma[15]; // unique variance for each species 1-15
  real<lower = 0, upper = 100> sispp; 
  real<lower = 0, upper = 100> siplot; 
}

transformed parameters{
  vector[N] mu;
  vector[N] sigmavector; //create vector of variance values for model block
  
  for (i in 1:N){
    sigmavector[i] <- sigma[genus[i]]; 
    mu[i] <- alpha + beta*x[i] + plotran[plot[i]] + genran[genus[i]];
  }
}

model{
  alpha ~ normal(0, 1000);
  beta ~ normal(0, 1000);
  
  plotran ~ normal(0, siplot);
  genran ~ normal(0, sigen);
  
  y ~ normal(mu, sigmavector);
}

I have also attached a simple R script and data set that recreates the problem. -Devin

The simplest thing to do would be to provide a higher
lower bound in:
> real<lower = 0, upper = 100> sigma[15]; // unique variance for each species 1-15

This implicitly supposes a Uniform(0,100) prior on sigma,
and that doesn't sound reasonable given the data.

Ideally, you'd be able to fit a hierarchical model.
would look like something like this:

sigma ~ lognormal(mu_sigma,sigma_sigma);

and then you need priors on parameters mu_sigma and sigma_sigma.
But I have no idea if lognormal() is a good distribution. You
could just use a regular normal, too, given that the sigma are
already constrained to [0,100]. Or an inverse gamma distribution.
Hopefully, Andrew will weigh in with some more reasonable advice.

- Bob

If the sampler works, that's great. Any config will give
you proper samples from the posterior.

You might find it better to let NUTS do the heavy lifting
and just increase the acceptance probability target and
the treedepth if necessary.

But the bigger question is whether the estimates are
reasonable. It probably doesn't make sense to have the
sigma for a group be too low. A hierarchical model will
partially pool the estimates across groups, with how
much pooling determined by how much the groups vary.

- Bob

parts:
Devin,

Yes, indeed, I think it would be a good idea to reduce the scale on priors of the form U(0,100) or N(0,100^2). This won't solve all problems but it can't hurt.
If the issue is that the variance parameter can be very small in the estimation, yes, one approach would be to put in a prior that keeps the variance away from 0 (lognormal, gamma, whatever), another approach would be to use the Matt trick. Some mixture of these ideas might help.

And, by the way: when you do these things it might feel like an awkward bit of kluging to play around with the model to get it to convert properly. But the kluges of today are the textbook solutions of tomorrow. We're living in beta-test world when it comes to statistical modeling; we might as well enjoy it!

A

Ah.  There have been a lot of improvements since 1.3, consider updating!

I'd recommend changing to delta=0.8 (soon to be our new default) and even experiment in increasing that.  Also with a stepsize that small you're probably hitting the max_treedepth threshold, be sure to increase that as necessary.

But really the extremely small stepsize is indicative of a nasty posterior and tweaking your model can help a lot.  More informative priors makes a huge difference, as does non-centered parameterizations (the Matt trick).

I currently convert my group level variance to a vector that is the length of my data set in the transformed parameters block, so would I simply add a new parameter as a multiplier at this step? I also am not clear what types of priors I would then put on these parameters. Maybe I should also apply the Matt trick to the random effects here? I am really an ecologist, not a statistician, so I apologize if I am slow to understand the details, but I could use some help with the reparameterization. I will repost the simplified version of my model below. Tightening the priors is not a problem, though I tried this alone in the past without noticeable improvement.

  vector[15] sppran; //random effect of species

  real<lower = 0, upper = 100> sispp; 
  real<lower = 0, upper = 100> siplot; 
}

transformed parameters{
  vector[N] mu;
  vector[N] sigmavector; //create vector of variance values for model block
  
  for (i in 1:N){
sigmavector[i] <- sigma[genus[i]];  //Should this change to sigmavector[i] <- modifier*sigma[genus[i]]

mu[i] <- alpha + beta*x[i] + plotran[plot[i]] + genran[genus[i]];
  }
}

model{
  alpha ~ normal(0, 1000);
  beta ~ normal(0, 1000);
  
  plotran ~ normal(0, siplot);
  genran ~ normal(0, sigen);
  
  y ~ normal(mu, sigmavector);
}

On 11/22/13, 1:09 PM, Devin Leopold wrote:
> I did try to upgrade to 2.0.1, but discovered a bug with sd() in the transformed parameters block, which I am using in
> this model, so I had to revert to 1.3 (I reported this to Bob already).

I'm working on it right now. I'll go into our
next patch.

You'll get the same bug defining sd() yourself
as the square root of variance --- it's a problem
with the way the chain rule propagates through
sqrt(x + y + z) when x, y and z are all zero.

> You are correct, I did need to increase
> max_treedepth. I have been using max_treedepth=16, but I am a bit unclear if this is too high (I do not hit it,
> usually).

It can't be too high other than in terms of time.
But if you hit a high boundary, it indicates a really
nasty posterior. We set it to 10 by default as a compromise
so it didn't look like programs were going into infinite
loops when they tried 2^15 (32K) gradient calls.

> What is an acceptable amount for the sampler to be hitting the max tree depth? With these changes I have also
> found the model to be incredibly slow. I tried delta=0.65 max_treedepth=15 before bed last night and still have not
> finished 4k iterations, now 10hrs later. Is this slow speed expected with settings like this?

Time is proportional to 2^treedepth * number of iterations.
So yes, this is expected.

> I think Andrew was suggesting that I implement the Matt trick on the variance parameter in my model, but I am not
> completely clear how I would do that. I currently convert my group level variance to a vector that is the length of my
> data set in the transformed parameters block, so would I simply add a new parameter as a multiplier at this step?

Exactly. There's a chapter in the manual on transformations
and more info in the optimization chapter.

> I also
> am not clear what types of priors I would then put on these parameters.

The Matt trick doesn't change the model posterior that you
care about. But it does change the parameters involved in
the actual sampling, with the posterior you care about being
a transfrom of the actual parameters used.

> Maybe I should also apply the Matt trick to the
> random effects here? I am really an ecologist, not a statistician, so I apologize if I am slow to understand the
> details, but I could use some help with the reparameterization.

If you've gotten this far, you're doing statistics :-)

But I take your point. The only person on the Stan dev team
with a bona fide Ph.D. in stats is Andrew. The rest of
us are from a mix of computer science and physics and poli sci
backgrounds.

> I will repost the simplified version of my model below.
> Tightening the priors is not a problem, though I tried this alone in the past without noticeable improvement.
>
> parameters{
> real alpha;
> real beta;
> vector[15] sppran; //random effect of species
> vector[261] plotran; //random effect of plot
> real<lower = 0, upper = 100> sigma[15]; // unique variance for each species 1-15
> real<lower = 0, upper = 100> sispp;
> real<lower = 0, upper = 100> siplot;
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
> vector[N] mu;
> vector[N] sigmavector; //create vector of variance values for model block
> for (i in 1:N){
> sigmavector[i] <- sigma[genus[i]]; //Should this change to sigmavector[i] <- modifier*sigma[genus[i]]
> mu[i] <- alpha + beta*x[i] + plotran[plot[i]] + genran[genus[i]];
> }
> }
>
> model{
> alpha ~ normal(0, 1000);
> beta ~ normal(0, 1000);
> plotran ~ normal(0, siplot);
> genran ~ normal(0, sigen);
> y ~ normal(mu, sigmavector);
> }

Given that y's data, here's no recentering to do here.
At most you could rescale with:

parameters {
real alpha_raw;
...
transformed parameters {
real alpha;
alpha <- 1000 * alpha_raw;
...
model {
alpha ~ normal(0,1);

And similarly for the other parameters (using siplot and
sigen for plotran and genran).

Tightening the prior on alpha or beta (that is, reducing
that 1000 * to something smaller) would be beneficial if
there's not much data and you expect the value of alpha and
beta to be near 0.

The only reason to use a scale of 1000 is if 5000 and
-5000 are realistic values for alpha.

- Bob

>
> On Thursday, November 21, 2013 10:46:35 PM UTC-10, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
> Ah. There have been a lot of improvements since 1.3, consider updating!
>
> I'd recommend changing to delta=0.8 (soon to be our new default) and even experiment in increasing that. Also with
> a stepsize that small you're probably hitting the max_treedepth threshold, be sure to increase that as necessary.
>
> But really the extremely small stepsize is indicative of a nasty posterior and tweaking your model can help a lot.
> More informative priors makes a huge difference, as does non-centered parameterizations (the Matt trick).
>
